title: 10 Best Insurance Automation Tools and Software in 2026
summary: Compare the 10 best insurance automation tools for 2026: AI workspaces, IDP, RPA, low-code, and claims messaging, with real results and pricing.
body_markdown:
Insurance automation tools are software that take repetitive work off underwriters, claims teams, brokers, and operations staff: reading submissions, keying data into core systems, checking policies, routing claims, and answering status questions. In 2026, the category spans five kinds of product, from robotic process automation (RPA) bots to AI workspaces built specifically for insurance.


**The short answer:** the best insurance automation tool depends on the work you're automating. **FurtherAI** is the strongest choice for end-to-end commercial insurance workflows such as submissions, policy checking, claims intake, and audits. **Cytora** fits underwriting intake for large carriers, **Hyperscience** and **Indico Data** fit high-volume document extraction, **UiPath** , **Automation Anywhere** , and **Microsoft Power Automate** fit rules-based tasks across legacy systems, **Appian** and **Pega** fit case management, and **Hi Marley** fits claims communication. Many insurers end up combining two or three of these.


## **Key takeaways**


- **Insurance automation software comes in five types:** insurance-native AI workspaces, intelligent document processing (IDP), RPA and agentic automation, low-code process and case management, and communication automation.
- **Most insurers still automate tasks, not whole processes.** 71% of insurance leaders say they mainly use AI for content generation or routine task automation, and only 29% run front-to-back processes through AI agents or automation, according to[KPMG's September 2026 research](https://kpmg.com/xx/en/media/press-releases/2026/09/insurers-see-ai-leadership-gaps-remain.html) .
- **Agentic automation is moving fast at large carriers:** 74% of large P&C carriers were piloting agentic AI in 2026, up from 22% in 2025, per[Datos Insights](https://datos-insights.com/reports/insurance-technology-trends-2026-pc-insurers-ins-2025-102223/) .
- **Insurance-specific tools win on unstructured documents.** General RPA and workflow platforms are strong for structured, repeatable steps but need extra configuration to read submissions, loss runs, and policies.
- **Measure outcomes, not activity.** Track cycle time, touch time per file, accuracy, and straight-through processing before and after deployment.

## **What is insurance automation software?**


**Insurance automation software is any tool that completes insurance work with little or no manual effort** , such as extracting data from an ACORD form, clearing a submission against appetite, updating a policy record after an endorsement, or sending a claimant a status update. The work still happens under human oversight; the software handles the repetitive steps and routes exceptions to a person.


Older automation followed fixed rules: if a field says X, do Y. That works well on structured data and stable screens. It struggles with what insurance runs on: broker emails, statements of values (SOVs), loss runs, policy wordings, and medical records that arrive in a different layout every time. That's why newer tools add AI that reads documents from context, and why the market now splits into the five categories below.


Category What it automates best Where it needs help Tools in this guide


Insurance-native AI workspaces Full insurance workflows: reading, checking, summarizing, and routing submissions, policies, and claims Core transaction processing such as rating and billing stays in your policy system FurtherAI, Cytora


Intelligent document processing (IDP) Classifying documents and extracting fields from forms, scans, and attachments Insurance judgment steps (appetite, coverage gaps) usually need to be built around it Hyperscience, Indico Data


RPA and agentic automation Repetitive, rules-based tasks across legacy screens, now with AI agents for exceptions Unstructured documents and frequent screen changes UiPath, Automation Anywhere, Power Automate


Low-code process and case management Multi-step workflows with routing, approvals, SLAs, and case history Document understanding often comes from add-ons or partners Appian, Pega


Communication automation Policyholder and claimant conversations, status updates, and inbound inquiries Back-office document and data work Hi Marley


‍


If you're weighing a general-purpose tool against an insurance-specific one, our guide to[horizontal vs dedicated insurance AI platforms](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/insurance-ai-horizontal-vs-dedicated-platforms) walks through the trade-offs in more detail.


## **Why insurers are investing in automation in 2026**


The pressure is the same one underwriting and claims leaders have described for years: skilled people spend too much of their day on data work. Accenture's *Underwriting rewritten* research found that[more than a third of an underwriter's time still goes to non-core activities](https://insuranceblog.accenture.com/ai-underwriting-beyond-the-hype) such as data collection and administration.


What's changed is how quickly insurers are moving from pilots to production. **Insurers move 62% of AI pilots into production, more than any other industry among the five EXL surveyed** in[EXL's 2026 Enterprise AI Study](https://www.exlservice.com/insights/reports-research/ai-insurance-adoption-lasting-advantage) . Agentic AI is now being piloted at most large carriers, as the chart below shows.


‍


Results still lag the activity. KPMG found that only 11% of insurance leaders have a very clear view of the return on their AI investment, and nearly half of AI budgets go to operational and back-office efficiency,[according to the same KPMG report](https://kpmg.com/xx/en/media/press-releases/2026/09/insurers-see-ai-leadership-gaps-remain.html) . The IBM Institute for Business Value reports that[just 12% of insurers have embedded AI across core operations with consistently high returns](https://riskandinsurance.com/only-12-of-insurers-are-cashing-in-on-a-i-but-they-are-pulling-far-ahead/) , and that those insurers embed it directly into claims, fraud, and underwriting workflows rather than running it as a standalone tool. The lesson for tool selection: pick software that runs inside real workflows and reports measurable outcomes.


## **How we chose these insurance automation tools**


We looked at tools insurers can buy today and evaluated each one on five criteria:


1. **Insurance workflow fit:** how much of a real insurance process (submission, policy, claim, audit) the tool can automate.
2. **Handling of unstructured documents:** how well it reads the emails, PDFs, spreadsheets, and scans insurance runs on.
3. **Controls:** human-in-the-loop review, audit trails, and governance for regulated work.
4. **Integration:** documented connections to core, agency, and productivity systems.
5. **Public proof:** named or described insurance customers with published outcomes.


Customer outcomes below come from vendor case studies, customer announcements, or trade press, and are labeled as reported. Results depend on your documents, systems, and volumes, so test any shortlisted tool on your own files.


## **The 10 best insurance automation tools in 2026**


### 1. FurtherAI: best for end-to-end commercial insurance workflows

Where RPA moves data between screens, FurtherAI reads and reasons over the insurance documents themselves, such as SOVs with tens of thousands of locations, loss runs, and multi-version policy wordings, and then hands a reviewed, source-cited result to the person who owns the decision.

## **RPA vs IDP vs AI agents: which do insurers need?**


**Most insurers need more than one.** Each technology solves a different part of the problem:


- **RPA** repeats fixed steps across screens and systems. Use it for structured, stable tasks such as posting payments or copying data between systems.
- **IDP** turns documents into structured data. Use it when the bottleneck is reading forms, scans, and attachments.
- **AI agents** plan and carry out multi-step work, deciding what to do next within rules you set. Use them for workflows that vary from file to file, such as clearing a submission or triaging a claim, with people approving at defined checkpoints.


Insurance-native AI workspaces combine document understanding and agents with insurance context, so a single workflow can read a submission, check it against guidelines, and prepare it for an underwriter. Rules still matter after extraction: deterministic checks on totals, dates, and required fields catch errors before data moves downstream. We cover that hybrid pattern in[rules-based automation vs AI extraction](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/rules-based-automation-vs-ai-extraction-claims-documents) and agent by agent in[AI agents for insurance](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/ai-agents-for-insurance) .


## **How to choose insurance automation software**


‍


Criterion Question to ask What good looks like


Workflow coverage How much of the process does it finish without handoffs? Handles the whole workflow, with people approving exceptions


Document accuracy Does it read our real submissions, loss runs, and claim files? Field-level accuracy measured on your own documents, not a demo set


Traceability Can a reviewer see where each value came from? Every field links to its source page


Controls and audit Who approved what, and when? Logged decisions, overrides, and versions


Integration Does it connect to our core, agency, and email systems? Documented connectors and write-back, not only exports


Time to value How long until production? A first workflow live in weeks, with a clear pilot plan


Maintenance What breaks when a form or screen changes? No template or bot rebuild for every new layout


Governance Does it support our AI policy and regulator expectations? Fits frameworks such as the NAIC Model Bulletin on insurers' use of AI


‍


Governance is worth checking early. ## **How much does insurance automation software cost?**


Pricing depends on the category. **Low-code RPA tools publish per-seat and per-bot prices:** Microsoft Power Automate Premium is $15 per user per month and Power Automate Process is $150 per bot per month, billed annually, as stated on[Microsoft's pricing page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/products/power-automate/pricing/) . **Enterprise RPA, IDP, case management, and insurance-native AI platforms are quote-based** , and are usually priced on volume (documents, submissions, or claims), users, workflows, or a platform fee.


License cost is only part of the total. Budget for implementation, integration, testing on your own documents, change management, and ongoing maintenance, which is higher for screen-based bots. For cost ranges, pricing models, and proof-of-concept terms, see[AI for insurance operations: costs and ROI](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/the-real-roi-of-ai-in-commercial-insurance-operations) .


## **How to roll out insurance automation**


1. **Pick one workflow with a clear owner.** Submission intake, policy checking, or claim intake are common first choices.
2. **Measure the baseline.** Record cycle time, touch time per file, error rate, and backlog before you start.
3. **Pilot on real documents.** Use a representative sample, including the messy files, and agree on what "correct" looks like.
4. **Keep people on exceptions.** Route low-confidence results and rule failures to reviewers, and log every decision.
5. **Scale to the next workflow.** Reuse the same integrations and controls so each new workflow goes live faster.

## **Frequently asked questions**


#### What is insurance automation software?


Insurance automation software completes repetitive insurance work with little manual effort, such as extracting data from submissions, clearing risks against appetite, updating policy records, comparing policies, and routing claims. It includes five main types: insurance-native AI workspaces, intelligent document processing, RPA and agentic automation, low-code process and case management, and communication automation. People stay in charge of decisions and exceptions, while the software handles the data work.


#### What are the best insurance automation tools in 2026?


The leading insurance automation tools in 2026 are FurtherAI, Cytora, Hyperscience, Indico Data, UiPath, Automation Anywhere, Microsoft Power Automate, Appian, Pega, and Hi Marley. FurtherAI is the strongest choice for end-to-end commercial insurance workflows. RPA tools such as UiPath suit rules-based tasks across legacy systems, IDP tools suit high-volume document extraction, and Hi Marley suits claims communication. The right pick depends on which workflow you automate first.


#### What's the difference between RPA, IDP, and AI agents in insurance?


RPA repeats fixed steps across screens and systems, so it suits structured, stable tasks like posting payments. IDP reads documents and turns them into structured data. AI agents carry out multi-step work that changes from file to file, such as clearing a submission, within rules you set and with people approving at checkpoints. Many insurers combine all three, often inside an insurance-native AI workspace.


#### Which insurance processes should be automated first?


Start with high-volume, document-heavy work where the steps repeat: submission intake and clearance, policy checking and comparison, FNOL and claim intake, endorsements, and underwriting audits. These workflows have clear baselines, such as minutes per submission or hours per audit, so you can measure results quickly. Pick one workflow with a single owner, pilot it on real documents, and expand once the numbers hold up.


#### How much does insurance automation software cost?


Costs vary by category. Microsoft Power Automate publishes list prices of $15 per user per month for Premium and $150 per bot per month for Process. Most enterprise RPA, document processing, and insurance-native AI platforms are quote-based and priced on volume, users, workflows, or a platform fee. Also budget for implementation, integration, testing, and ongoing maintenance, which can exceed license costs for screen-based bots.


#### Can insurance automation tools work with legacy core systems?


Yes. Most insurance automation tools sit alongside existing policy, claims, and agency systems instead of replacing them. RPA works through the user interface, while AI workspaces, IDP, and process platforms connect through APIs, connectors, and email. Ask each vendor for documented integrations with your specific systems, how data is written back, and what happens when a screen or form changes.


#### How do you measure the ROI of insurance automation?


Measure the workflow before and after deployment. Track cycle time, touch time per file, accuracy or error rate, straight-through processing, backlog, and hours redeployed to higher-value work such as underwriting or claims investigation. Compare those gains with license, implementation, and maintenance costs. Few insurers do this well today: only 11% of insurance leaders say they have a very clear view of their AI return, according to KPMG.
